Symplectic redistribution ​

The factorisation lemma characterises the symplectic redistributions: a canonical map of and a free choice of the weights. This chapter asks what such a map can achieve. Five facts decide it, and each construction of the manual is shaped by them:

  1. for a finite marker set, symplecticity alone restricts almost nothing; the content is that one smooth map, with few parameters, moves all markers (finite marker sets);

  2. a canonical map that is the same for every marker moves a hole but keeps its volume (Liouville); this includes every map generated by a Hamiltonian that does not depend on the weights (one map for all markers);

  3. a Hamiltonian that depends on the weights compresses the marker density at a rate given by a Poisson bracket with the weight field (weight-dependent Hamiltonians);

  4. a weight tied to a density at the new velocity folds the velocity–momentum relation, so the new state is computed from , never from (the fold);

  5. parameters computed from the markers make the map symplectic only for their frozen values, unless they satisfy a variational closure (state-dependent parameters).

Finite marker sets ​

For a finite marker set, symplecticity alone imposes nothing on the final positions. The translations   ,    with constants , and   are canonical, conserve , and map any configuration to any other, so any target configuration is the image of a canonical map whose parameters are computed from the data. The condition has content in two cases. Either the map is exactly symplectic as a function of the full state, as the gauge step and the elementary maps are. Or one smooth map with few parameters, in the variables , moves all markers, as the physical evolution does. The rest of this chapter works out the consequences of the second case.

Liouville's theorem for the marker density ​

Let the markers have a smooth density  , the number of markers per unit volume, and a smooth weight field  , so that the represented density is   : the weight in a small region is    . The sheet map     carries the markers to canonical coordinates, where they have a density (see the fold for in terms of and ).

Let be a canonical map of the single-marker space , the same for all markers. It carries the markers in a region to and preserves the volume,  , so the marker count   for every gives the transported canonical density

This is Liouville's theorem for the marker density. Its consequence for a hole — a region in which is small — is that moves the hole but keeps its volume: the level sets     have the volumes of the level sets of , for every . A smooth canonical map applied to every marker therefore rearranges the canonical marker density; it cannot fill a hole. It can only move it, for example into the tails of , where few markers are needed. The canonical transport of the first construction states the condition precisely (the limit of equidistribution).

Holes persist ​

Corollary (holes persist)

Under the assumptions of the proposition, let   be an open set that contains no marker . Then contains no marker , and  . If the markers sample a density on , the new markers sample  , and the volume   of every superlevel set is invariant.

Proof

If  , then   , a contradiction. A symplectic map preserves the Liouville volume. The density statement is the transformation rule of a density under a volume-preserving map.

A mean-field Hamiltonian therefore only rearranges the marker density in . It cannot fill a hole, and it cannot change the distribution of the density values. This holds independently of how the parameters were chosen. The corollary keeps the volume of a hole, not its shape: an area-preserving map can stretch a hole into a thin band, which reduces the largest empty disk while the empty volume stays the same. To carry the statement over to , consider the chart  , where is a smooth field of weights. Where is a diffeomorphism onto its image, it maps holes to holes. A gauge step with a smooth weight field therefore leaves a hole open in too.

The example of mean_field_example has 274 markers on a jittered lattice with a disk cut out, the moments     and the single-marker Hamiltonian      , nonlinear in the moments. Its single-marker Hamiltonian is     (mean_field_single_hamiltonian). One step of symplectic Euler or of the implicit midpoint rule with   on the whole ensemble agrees with the single-marker map to   while the markers move up to ;    ; the area of the hole is unchanged, and no marker lies in its image. The control, a weight-dependent Hamiltonian     with two coincident markers of the weights and , maps them to points apart, so no single map exists (test/projection/structure.jl).

Uncoupled maps ​

The simplest single-marker map is the one that does not couple the markers at all.

Proposition (obstruction for uncoupled maps)

Let be a symplectic diffeomorphism of   and let   for every marker. If an open set   holds no marker , then holds no marker , and  . With equal output weights   the hole of the markers in keeps its volume .

Proof

The first part is the corollary holes persist for  . With  ,  , a linear map of determinant .

A canonical map of all markers keeps the volume of , not that of , so a map that couples the markers — other than through a mean field — is free of this obstruction. The constructions leave it in two ways. A Hamiltonian that depends on the weights moves markers of different weights with different maps (the next section; the Hamiltonian particle projection). A Hamiltonian or a map that couples the markers through their order or their pairs breaks the single-marker form (the pairwise Hamiltonians of the spline-projection redistribution, which also explain why uncoupled control Hamiltonians and the subtraction of a mean force fail, and the slices of the sliced redistribution).

The velocity–momentum fold ​

A redistribution that ties the new weight to a density at the new velocity meets a fold. Fix a position , a volume   and a density   , and let the weight of a marker at be   . Its momentum is then a function of its velocity,

The same relation appears in three places: as the sheet map     of a smooth weight field (with   ); as the implicit weight   that requirement (R3) suggests at fixed (with  ); and as the weight of a target point in the spline-projection redistribution.

The sheet. For a smooth weight field the sheet map has, at fixed , the derivative    in one dimension. Under the single-sheet condition   it is a diffeomorphism onto its image that preserves the sign of , and counting the markers in a region in two ways,      , gives the canonical marker density

The single-sheet condition holds for equal weights, the case of markers loaded with density  . It fails for uniformly loaded markers with   and a Maxwellian : the sheet folds at  . A folded sheet consists of several layers in , each of which is transported separately; the canonical transport treats one layer. Markers equidistributed in with weights have a density in that is singular on the image of the fold.

The consequence for every construction. A canonical momentum above has no velocity, and every momentum below it has at least a subthermal and a suprathermal one. A construction therefore never computes first and then solves for . It specifies — a target point — and evaluates the weight and the momentum   forward, uniquely and smoothly across all velocities, the suprathermal tail included. The Hamiltonian particle projection takes the new weight from a target point; the spline-projection redistribution weighs its relaxed targets.

velocity_fold_momentum evaluates , velocity_fold_determinant the determinant with by automatic differentiation, and maxwellian_fold_momentum_bound the bound . The figure shows, for  ,   and  , (a) the momentum of a marker whose weight is tied to the Maxwellian, bounded by (dotted) and turning back on the thermal sphere (dashed), and (b) the determinant  , which vanishes there and is negative on the suprathermal velocities (shaded). The momentum of has a second, suprathermal velocity, which bisection on finds:

julia
P(v) = velocity_fold_momentum(f, v; m = m, ΔΩ = ΔΩ)
function suprathermal_preimage(P, target, lo, hi)
    for _ in 1:200
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        P(mid) > target ? (lo = mid) : (hi = mid)
    end
    lo
end
v2 = suprathermal_preimage(P, P(0.5vth), vth, 10vth)
(subthermal = 0.5vth, suprathermal = v2, momentum = (P(0.5vth), P(v2)))
(subthermal = 0.65, suprathermal = 2.0908037784604656, momentum = (0.17208689600399615, 0.17208689600399624))

Parameters that depend on the state ​

Every construction of the manual computes something from the markers: stretches, parameters of a Hamiltonian, slices, multipliers. This section states what that does to symplecticity.

Two readings of symplecticity ​

The factorisation lemma answers the question for the form , in which the weights are coordinates. The dynamics does not preserve this form. For free streaming,   , one 1D-1V marker gives     and     , so that

The pull-back residual of free streaming over   is , the entry of  :

julia
stream(z) = [z[1] + 0.9z[2], z[2], z[3]]
(pullback_residual(stream, [0.3, -1.2, 0.8]; m = 1.7), 1.7 * 0.9 * 1.2)
(1.8359999999991423, 1.8359999999999999)

The flow of the Hamiltonian preserves only for fixed weights. In the coordinates it is a Poisson map of the bracket

for which every is a Casimir. A Poisson map sends Casimirs to functions of Casimirs, so in this reading a redistribution may change the weights only as  .

The two readings lead to the following practical statement. A redistribution of the form followed by a gauge step is symplectic for , and between two redistributions the dynamics is symplectic for with the weights of that interval. As soon as the new weights, or the parameters of , depend on the state, the composition "flow, redistribution, flow" is not a canonical map of the initial data. This is the same situation as an adaptive time step that depends on the state. What a symplectic redistribution does deliver is a map that does not coarse-grain: it keeps exactly (the gauge step) or moves them canonically (), and it introduces no numerical diffusion. The composition defect of the sliced redistribution measures the effect for one later flow step.

Frozen and closed-loop parameters ​

Let be a family of symplectic maps of with a parameter vector . A solver that determines   from the ensemble produces the map  , with the Jacobian

The second term destroys the symplecticity of in general. Two maps must therefore be distinguished: the open-loop map with frozen, which is symplectic by construction, and the closed-loop map , in which a perturbation of the incoming ensemble also perturbs the solved parameters, as the multiplier variations do in projected variational integrators (Kraus, 2017). For maps that are one step of a parametrised Hamiltonian, the defect has an exact form.

The same holds for a type-2 generating function with fixed by  : with  , the stationarity gives   and  , so generates the same map. A stationarity condition is a property of the generating function, however; it cannot express a fit of the image points to targets.

The constructions of the manual therefore use parameter-wise symplecticity: for every frozen value of the stretches, the parameters, the slices or the multipliers, the map is exactly symplectic, and these values are computed from the markers. The gauge rezoning is the exception: its stretches may depend on the state in any way, because the gauge step is symplectic for every . The closed loops of the spline-projection redistribution evaluate both sides of the identity (closed_loop_defect) for a target-matching closure and a variational one.
